title: Former Sault man shot and killed by police in Calgary ; POLICE: Officer says he was forced to shoot
article: Jonathan Rawlings' drug addiction, depression and repeated return to crime put him face-to-face with a police officer who said he was forced to shoot when the 36-year-old came at him with a weapon.
Rawlings was once a Sault Ste. Marie resident, says the the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team, which is Alberta's equivalent of Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU).
Several friends claim he was not a hardened criminal, but a man who often surrounded himself with "the wrong people," rather than those who could put him on the right path he so desperately sought.

"Why on earth if he was trying to change his life and he was getting out of remand, was he jumping into stolen vehicles?" said a man who didn't want to be named and became friends with Rawlings when they both did time at Drumheller. "I'm not going to justify his actions, but why couldn't he just give himself up?" Police ask the same question.
They said Rawlings, with a woman apparently unwittingly involved in the ordeal, was spotted in a stolen truck by patrol officers Wednesday.

Cops followed covertly in unmarked units and a HAWCS chopper. They said at some point Rawlings and a man in another stolen truck drove in tandem before police put out a spike belt and approached. That's when, according to police, Rawlings and the other two instead of surrendering fled in the other truck.
A short time later, officers moved in when Rawlings and the woman bailed and within minutes he was dead.
Police Chief Rick Hanson defended the actions of the officer who he said chased him, only to be confronted by Rawlings who threatened him with a weapon which turned out to be a screwdriver.

Chelsea Springman was devastated to learn her friend's life ended in such a senseless way -- days after she spoke to him for what would be the final time. "He seemed disappointed in himself," she said Friday. "He said it was hard to talk to people, they were moving on with life and he was still doing the same thing, running with criminals... he just got caught up with the wrong people and had no family here ... He said it made him feel bad and he wanted to make a change."
That seemed to be an ongoing struggle.

Rawlings was handed a 3 1/2 year jail term he began in 2006 on charges including drug possession and possession for the purpose of trafficking with Parole Board of Canada documents showing he struggled with addictions and the death of a fiancé which led to depression, job loss and all culminated in a return to crime.

Amanda Bennett said Rawlings said he was a man with "a big heart but did some really stupid things." She worried about what would become of her one-time beau if he didn't make some changes. "Either he would go back to jail, have a crummy life, OD on drugs or maybe get killed by the wrong people," she said. "It seemed, eventually something would happen ... I don't know what the heck he was thinking." She understands police might have had no other option than to open fire.
"I think there was panic on both sides, mistakes on both sides. The fact is, Johnny has to pay with his life. It is what it is. No one is to blame and only that police officer knows what happened."
His jailhouse friend, who hasn't returned to crime himself, said Rawlings was a good man who made some bad choices. "No matter what the circumstances in the end it's a tragedy," he said.
